claims.text: The as-processed HfNbTiVAl10 has an engineered hierarchical heterostructure with controlled grain sizes and phase distributions.
A model integrating high-resolution microstructural imaging, effective-medium methods, and machine-learning regression can predict the mechanical behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
Multiscale grain-size distributions, phase-interface characteristics, and precipitate arrangements are relevant structural mediators of the predicted mechanical response.
Detailed microstructural descriptors can be used to estimate local stress-concentration factors.
Detailed microstructural descriptors can be used to estimate load-transfer pathways.
Effective-medium approximations combined with machine-learning regression can upscale the microstructural descriptors to predict elastic and plastic responses.
The proposed framework reduces reliance on computationally intensive full-field simulations.
The model will predict Young's modulus within approximately 5–10% of experimental measurements.
The model will predict yield strength within approximately 5–10% of experimental measurements.
The model will predict fracture-related properties within approximately 5–10% of experimental measurements.
The model will reduce computational time by approximately 50–70% relative to established simulation techniques.
Existing state-of-the-art finite-element and full-field simulations typically have error margins of 10–15%.
Existing finite-element and full-field simulations have significantly higher computational costs than the proposed model.
The model may fail when imaged hierarchical features omit dominant load-bearing features because of unanticipated defects or imaging limitations.
The model may fail when dynamic phase transformations or other unmodeled mechanisms govern material behavior.
Predictive accuracy and computational savings may vary with specimen quality, imaging resolution, and calibration-dataset representativeness.
Deviation greater than 10% from independent measurements, when established simulations achieve error at or below 10%, is the predeclared decisive falsification outcome.
